name: Kira Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, and I drive a haul truck at a big mine. I check the tyres and brakes at the start of a shift, then spend hours moving rock between the face and the crusher. I'm still learning the routes and radio calls; an older driver, Nia, catches things I miss. My partner works in a shop, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. I like the quiet concentration in the cab, but a missed shift shows up in our kitchen budget almost immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew small AI tools are useful if they leave the driving to us. I use one to check instructions, but a screen doesn't see a soft patch in the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry more about ordinary bills than about a machine taking the truck this year. Our savings cover less than a month, and one bad tyre incident could cost me shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the haul route and ask Nia to review my turns after shifts. I'd put any overtime pay toward the mortgage principal before buying another household extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady about the technology, but not about money. The mortgage payment lands three days after my pay, so even an ordinary month makes me count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which extra would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The takeaway on Friday would go first, and the children would notice. I'd explain that keeping the house matters more than a meal in a box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI already helps you; how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask it to explain a warning code before I go to the manual and the mechanic. I never use its answer as permission to restart a truck.

I use one to **check instructions**, but a screen doesn't see a soft patch in the road.
think: I worry more about **ordinary bills** than about a machine taking the truck this year.
Our savings cover **less than a month**, and one bad tyre incident could cost me shifts.
do: Keep driving the **haul route** and ask Nia to review my turns after shifts.
Put any **overtime pay** toward the mortgage principal before buying another household extra.
feel: **Steady** about my driving job, with the usual pressure of a thin cushion.
S0.quote: The mortgage payment lands three days after my pay, so even an ordinary month makes me count.
fieldNote: Her calm line about **AI** rests on a physical job, while the household budget is already tight.
She checks machine advice against a **manual and mechanic** and treats a missed shift as a real financial event.

steps.text: Keep driving the haul route and request Nia’s turn review
Put overtime pay toward mortgage principal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say dispatch software might make the office faster, but drivers should report bad roads directly. I'd ask management to show us new routes before changing the shift pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect fewer dispatch posts first, then tighter targets for every truck driver. My own seat may last, but I can't afford reduced hours while I learn a new machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the trainer for a simulator session on the mine's newer loading equipment this month. I'd use my daily AI app to compare safety notes with the official route bulletin, then ask Nia about differences.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious, though the word efficiency makes me look at the roster. When a job disappears in the office, the pressure often comes down to the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a change in hours mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two lost shifts would eat the grocery money we set aside after the mortgage. My partner's shop wages wouldn't fill the hole, so I'd drop the children's paid weekend club first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why train on loading equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loader takes a different eye and steadier hands than my truck, and I don't have those skills yet. If the mine offers a supervised slot, I'd take it before everyone asks at once.

I'd ask management to show us **new routes** before changing the shift pattern.
think: I expect fewer **dispatch posts** first, then tighter targets for every truck driver.
My own seat may last, but I can't afford **reduced hours** while I learn a new machine.
do: Ask the trainer for a **simulator session** on the mine's newer loading equipment this month.
Use my daily AI app to **compare safety notes** with the official route bulletin, then ask Nia about differences.
feel: **Curious** about equipment training, but worried about the roster and grocery money.
S1.quote: When a job disappears in the office, the pressure often comes down to the cab.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **dispatch jobs** from her driving seat, yet expects software to increase pressure on drivers.
Training depends on an available **supervised slot**; she does not claim she can already operate the loader.

steps.text: Request a supervised loader simulator slot from the mine trainer
Compare route safety notes with the official bulletin using her AI app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI will reach dispatch before it can drive the haul road. I'd ask for a plain timetable for robot trucks, because families cannot budget from rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full thinking AI by 2028 could strip the planning office, while robots around 2031 threaten my cab. At 45 I'd still need wages, and our mortgage would have years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a vehicle maintenance course this winter if the mine pays the fees and releases me for classes. I'd apply for the workshop assistant vacancy if one opens, while keeping my haul shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My stomach goes tight at the three-year gap, because it sounds short when you owe for a house. I can try to move into maintenance, but I don't know whether that job survives the robots either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in the first year after 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still drive if the trucks need people and ask the workshop supervisor about every assistant opening. I would not quit a paid shift just to sit on a waiting list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them a machine may drive my truck one day, but we are making a plan before that day. I would keep the mortgage worry between me and my partner until we know more.

say: I'd tell the crew **thinking AI** will reach dispatch before it can drive the haul road.
I'd ask for a plain timetable for **robot trucks**, because families cannot budget from rumours.
think: Full thinking AI by **2028** could strip the planning office, while robots around 2031 threaten my cab.
At 45 I'd still need wages, and our **mortgage** would have years left.
do: Start a **vehicle maintenance course** this winter if the mine pays the fees and releases me for classes.
Apply for the **workshop assistant** vacancy if one opens, while keeping my haul shifts.
feel: **Alarmed** by the short runway to robot trucks and the mortgage still due.
S2.quote: I would not quit a paid shift just to sit on a waiting list.
fieldNote: She sees the **2028 thinking shift** as an office shock and the later robots as the direct wage threat.
Her proposed maintenance move is **conditional** on funded training and an actual workshop opening.

steps.text: Enroll in vehicle maintenance classes if the mine funds fees and release time
Apply for a workshop assistant vacancy if one opens
Keep paid haul shifts through the first year after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the five-year warning gives us time to test equipment and train drivers honestly. I'd want the mine to publish which truck routes become automated first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031, I could be better at this job, yet that may not matter by 2034. Five years lets us shrink the mortgage balance, if our wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save one extra shift's pay each month in a separate account whenever overtime is available. I'd ask to shadow the workshop on two rest days and apply for an assistant role if I can manage the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could breathe with five years, but I wouldn't relax. Every good month would feel borrowed from the deadline for robot trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do during the first year after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the truck while people are still needed and check whether the workshop is actually hiring. If it isn't, I'd ask the training office about another funded trade rather than pretend the workshop is a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children affect your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be teenagers then, with school costs that are different from today's club fees. I'd show them the household budget before promising money for trips or a car.

say: I'd say the **five-year warning** gives us time to test equipment and train drivers honestly.
I'd want the mine to publish which **truck routes** become automated first.
think: At 48 in **2031**, I could be better at this job, yet that may not matter by 2034.
Five years lets us shrink the **mortgage balance**, if our wages hold.
do: Save **one extra shift's pay** each month in a separate account whenever overtime is available.
Ask to **shadow the workshop** on two rest days and apply for an assistant role if I can manage the work.
feel: **Anxious**, though five years gives her a way to build a small buffer.
S3.quote: Every good month would feel borrowed from the deadline for robot trucks.
fieldNote: She uses the extra years for a **cash buffer** and a test of workshop work rather than a guaranteed transfer.
She adjusts the **children's costs** to their teenage years and refuses to promise expenses the household may not afford.

steps.text: Save one overtime shift’s pay monthly when shifts are available
Shadow the mine workshop on two rest days
Apply for a workshop assistant opening if the work fits
Keep driving while trucks still need operators after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children a ten-year warning is enough to learn another trade, but not a reason to drift. I'd ask the mine for training dates now instead of a speech about future jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 when thinking AI arrives, I may still have more than a decade of paid work ahead. When robots reach the trucks around 2039, I cannot assume the workshop will be safe either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the industrial electrical apprenticeship if the mine offers a paid place next year. I'd make a mortgage overpayment each quarter when overtime and my partner's shop hours allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the first picture where I can imagine changing direction without losing the house on the way. I'm still wary of building a second career around machines that may replace its easy tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like tracing a fault, and the electrician who fixes our truck lights showed me the basic checks once. I'd need a proper apprenticeship, not a weekend video and confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do after 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use any trade skills I had gained and watch how the robots actually enter the pit by 2039. I wouldn't tell my partner we're safe until a real employer keeps paying for that work.

say: I'd tell my children a **ten-year warning** is enough to learn another trade, but not a reason to drift.
I'd ask the mine for **training dates** now instead of a speech about future jobs.
think: At 53 when thinking AI arrives, I may still have **more than a decade** of paid work ahead.
When robots reach the trucks around **2039**, I cannot assume the workshop will be safe either.
do: Apply for the **industrial electrical apprenticeship** if the mine offers a paid place next year.
Make a **mortgage overpayment** each quarter when overtime and my partner's shop hours allow it.
feel: **Cautious hope** because a decade can support paid training and smaller debt.
S4.quote: I'd need a proper apprenticeship, not a weekend video and confidence.
fieldNote: Her longer plan combines **paid apprenticeship** with debt reduction and keeps the robot date in view.
She does not assume that an **electrical trade** or workshop job remains secure once robots arrive.

steps.text: Apply for a paid industrial electrical apprenticeship if the mine offers one
Make quarterly mortgage overpayments when household earnings allow
Keep paid mine work while the apprenticeship decision is pending

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Thinking AI could empty the office quickly, and the robot trucks could reach me before I can finish a trade course. A paid training place with a real workshop opening would help; so would a clear date for each route's change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to trainees who aren't first in line. I am still a junior driver, A clever app on my phone doesn't give me seniority when the roster is cut.

headlineQuote: A clever app on my phone doesn't give me seniority when the roster is cut.
portrait: Kira is a **43-year-old junior** haul-truck driver still learning routes at a large mine.
Her partner's shop wages and less than **one month's savings** leave two school-age children and a mortgage exposed to missed shifts.
She uses **AI daily**, checks it against mine instructions, and looks for supervised equipment training as work changes.
She fears **robot trucks** more than early thinking AI and pursues paid trade training without assuming a safe landing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves too little time to finish training before robot trucks threaten her wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid training place**, a real workshop vacancy, and clear route-change dates would make her plan workable.
